title: THE GROUND FLOOR · GET-UPS & LOCOMOTION
vibe: yellow · ground-based · 50 minutes · effort measured in quality and distance, not on a clock
why: Yesterday you did the whole Singapore Opener and pressed the 20, which answers the one question that session asked and resets the loading for the rest of this trip: 20 kg is your working single bell now, and the 16 drops to being the volume and skill bell. So the strength ceiling goes up. What does not go up today is leg impact. You slept six and your legs are still on the wrong side of twelve time zones, and yesterday already put fifteen minutes of running fused into a lift block. Running that same fused shape again is the one thing that would make this feel like a program that stopped paying attention. Today jumps as far away from it as the library allows. This is a ground day, and it is the shape this log has never once run. Scroll back through a month of sessions and you will find carries, get-ups and crawls scattered as finishers and filler, never as the session itself. The get-up is the single most neglected pattern in your entire history. Today it is the main course. The research lens behind this is Original Strength, which has not been pulled since 07-14 and is the tradition that actually speaks to what is wrong with you this morning. Their whole argument is that the developmental sequence, rolling and rocking and crawling and the contra-lateral gait pattern underneath all of it, is not a warm-up genre but a way of putting a nervous system back where it belongs. Which is a fairly precise description of what a long-haul flight takes out of you. The run stays, because it always stays, but it moves to the front as a twelve-minute flush at your own easy pace, and then the treadmill is done and your feet are on the floor for the rest of the hour.

blocks.title: WARM-UP · PRESS RESET
blocks.meta: ~8 min · floor · Moves Method Day C flow + the five Original Strength resets · one continuous sequence, nothing held

items.name: DIAPHRAGM BREATHING · 10 breaths
items.detail: On your back, knees bent, one hand on the belly and one on the chest. Ten breaths where only the bottom hand moves, nose in, long slow nose out. This is the first of the five resets and it is the one people skip. After a flight and a short night it is also the one doing the most work.

items.name: HEAD NODS AND NECK CIRCLES · 30 sec
items.detail: Face down propped on your elbows. Nod yes slowly, then no, then slow circles each direction. Small range, no forcing. Original Strength calls head control a reset because the vestibular system drives everything downstream of it, and that system is exactly what got scrambled crossing twelve time zones.

items.name: SEGMENTAL ROLLING · 4 each way
items.detail: On your back. Roll to your stomach leading with one arm only, legs completely passive. Then the other arm. Then lead with one leg, arms passive. Four total each direction. If a roll stalls halfway, that side is the stiff side, do two extra there. Do not cheat it with momentum.

items.name: ROCKING · 20 reps
items.detail: Hands and knees, hips back toward the heels and return, spine long. Twenty. Then ten more with the toes tucked under, which will find your calves and plantar fascia after a day of sitting.

items.name: CROSS-CRAWL, STANDING · 30 sec
items.detail: Standing, opposite elbow to opposite knee, marching. Thirty seconds building to a decent tempo. This is the contra-lateral gait pattern the whole system is built around and it is the bridge into the run.

items.name: BABY CRAWL · 2 x 15 m
items.detail: Hands and knees, opposite hand and opposite knee moving together, head up, breathing through the nose. Two lengths of whatever clear floor the gym has. Slow. This doubles as the rehearsal for Block 3, so pay attention to how the pattern feels now versus how it feels an hour from now.

blocks.text: This is Day C off the Moves Method menu, the continuous flow version, and it is the correct match for a ground-based session. It is also the only warm-up in the rotation that is itself an Original Strength sequence, which is why the lens and the warm-up are the same thing today instead of two separate ideas bolted together.

blocks.title: THE FLUSH · EASY CONTINUOUS RUN
blocks.meta: 12 min · treadmill · zero incline · one speed, set it and leave it
blocks.format: continuous aerobic, no intervals, no clock beyond the twelve minutes

items.name: RUN · 12:00 @ 12.2 to 12.9 km/h
items.detail: That is 4:55 to 4:40 per kilometre, or 7:55 to 7:30 per mile. Your own easy band straight off your watch history. Pick a number inside it, set the belt, and do not touch the console again for twelve minutes. Cadence quick, around 168 to 172, short steps. This is the entire treadmill portion of the day and it goes first on purpose, because after a flight the legs move better once blood has been through them, and everything after this is on the floor.

items.name: READ THE BELT WHEN YOU STOP
items.detail: Write down the distance number. Yesterday's three by four minutes should have put roughly 3.1 to 3.3 km on it and we never got the readout. Twelve minutes at a fixed speed is the cleanest possible calibration test for this machine, and once we know what its km/h actually delivers, every run for the rest of the trip gets prescribed off a real number instead of a converted guess.

blocks.text: The run is a fixed input in this program and it is not a slot to be justified. What changes is style. Yesterday it was three fused four-minute pieces inside a lift block. Today it is one uninterrupted continuous piece at the front of the session and then the treadmill is finished. Twelve minutes at your easy pace is roughly a mile and a half, which is deliberately shorter than your habitual two, because the volume of the day is going somewhere else entirely.

blocks.title: BLOCK 1 · THE DESCENDING LADDER · GET-UPS
blocks.meta: ~15 min · 16 kg bell · descending ladder 3-2-1 per side, twice through · no clock, rest as needed
blocks.workRest: One rep is one full get-up, floor to standing to floor. Set the bell down between sides. Rest whenever the next rep would be worse than the last one.

items.name: WAVE 1 · 3 / 3, then 2 / 2, then 1 / 1 · 16 kg
items.detail: Three get-ups on the right, three on the left. Then two and two. Then one and one. Twelve get-ups. Full range every time: roll to elbow, to hand, sweep the leg through, hip up, stand, then reverse the whole thing under control. Eyes on the bell on the way up, and you can let them come off it on the way down once the arm is locked and honest.

items.name: WAVE 2 · 3 / 3, then 2 / 2, then 1 / 1 · 16 kg or 20 kg
items.detail: Second pass, same ladder. The 20 kg is now your proven working bell after yesterday, so if wave one moved cleanly, take the 20 for the threes and twos and see what a heavier get-up feels like. If the shoulder wanders or the hip stalls on the sweep, stay at 16 and get twelve more clean reps. Either answer is useful. Twenty-four total get-ups is a genuinely serious volume day for a pattern you have never trained as the main event.

items.name: WHY THIS IS THE MAIN BLOCK
items.detail: The get-up is the most neglected pattern in your entire log. It appears as one line inside a gauntlet, as filler in a circuit, never as the thing the session is about. It is also close to the perfect movement for this specific morning: it loads the shoulder overhead through full range, it is unapologetically a core exercise, it demands the exact rolling and rocking and vestibular work the warm-up just primed, and it puts almost nothing through your legs as impact.

blocks.text: Neupert's #5 runs this as a five-four-three-two-one hell ladder for fifteen minutes. Cut to a doubled three-two-one because the rep quality on a get-up falls off a cliff before the muscles do, and because six hours of sleep is not the night to find out where that cliff is. The descending shape is the point: the hardest set is the first one, while you are sharpest, and every set after it gets shorter.

blocks.title: BLOCK 2 · LOADED LOCOMOTION
blocks.meta: ~10 min · 20 kg bell + dumbbells + open floor · 3 rounds · this is the conditioning, there is no treadmill in it
blocks.format: carry and crawl circuit, measured in distance through space
blocks.workRest: Move continuously through the four pieces, rest 60 seconds at the end of each round. Distance is the unit, not reps and not minutes.

items.name: SUITCASE CARRY · 30 m per side · 20 kg
items.detail: One bell hanging at one side, walk thirty metres or the longest clear stretch the gym gives you, switch hands, walk back. Level shoulders, no lean toward the weight, no hitch in the hip. Walk like the loaded hand is empty. Every step is a rep of refusing to bend sideways.

items.name: FARMER CARRY · 30 m · dumbbells
items.detail: Both dumbbells, heavier than the pair you used for rows yesterday. Thirty metres. Tall, ribs down, grip crushing. Pick a load where the grip is the thing that ends the walk, not the posture. Grip and loaded-carry work is a confirmed favourite of yours and it has had no dedicated slot since 08-02.

items.name: BACKWARD BEAR CRAWL · 15 m  ·  WILDCARD
items.detail: Hands and feet, knees an inch off the floor, and crawl backwards. Not forwards. This is the wildcard and it has never appeared anywhere in this log. Reversing the direction flips the whole demand: the shoulders take the load in a position they never see, the quads and the anterior core light up, and the cross-body coordination gets genuinely difficult because you cannot see where you are going. Fifteen metres will feel a lot longer than fifteen metres. If the wrists complain, make fists and crawl on the knuckles.

items.name: OVERHEAD CARRY · 20 m per side · 16 kg
items.detail: One bell locked out overhead, bicep by the ear, walk twenty metres, switch, walk back. Use the 16 here, not the 20. Overhead carrying after two dozen get-ups is asking a lot of a shoulder and the point is a stable lockout for the full distance, not a heavier number. If the elbow bends or the bell drifts forward, stop, reset, finish the walk.

blocks.text: Original Strength's argument, and the reason the lens fits today, is that carrying and crawling are not accessories, they are the load-bearing version of the same developmental patterns the warm-up ran unloaded. So the conditioning stimulus today comes from moving weight through space rather than from a belt or a clock. Your heart rate will get where it needs to go. It will just get there sideways.

blocks.title: BLOCK 3 · MIDLINE · SHORT ON PURPOSE
blocks.meta: ~5 min · bodyweight · the standing end-of-session core block

items.name: DEAD BUG · 8 per side, 2 rounds
items.detail: On your back, low back pressed flat, opposite arm and opposite leg extending away slowly while the ribs stay down. Eight a side, twice. Slow is the whole exercise. The instant your low back lifts off the floor, shorten the range.

items.name: SIDE PLANK REACH-THROUGH · 8 per side, 2 rounds
items.detail: Side plank on the elbow, top arm reaching to the ceiling, then threading it under your torso and back. Eight a side, twice. Anti-rotation with actual rotation loaded on top of it.

blocks.text: The standing rule that every session closes with a dedicated midline block holds, but five minutes is the honest number today. Twenty-four get-ups and three rounds of suitcase and overhead carries already made this one of the most midline-loaded sessions in the log. Bolting ten more minutes of core onto the end would be running the ritual rather than reading the session.

blocks.title: COOLDOWN
blocks.meta: ~4 min · shoulders from the get-ups and the overhead walks, hips from the ground work, plus a body clock to argue with
blocks.text: Doorway or wall pec stretch, 45 seconds per side, after all that time under an overhead lockout. Child's pose with the arms walked out to one side then the other, 45 seconds each, which is a rocking reset held still. Half-kneeling hip flexor stretch, 45 seconds per side. Then finish with two minutes of slow nasal breathing lying on your back, longer out than in. That last piece is not filler on a six-hour night after crossing twelve time zones. It is the first reset from the warm-up, run again at the other end, and it is the cheapest thing available for pushing a body clock in the right direction.

timer.emomUnit: No EMOM, no AMRAP, no rounds-for-time anywhere today. This is a deliberately timer-free session and effort is measured in rep quality and metres covered. Use the countdown once, for the twelve-minute run. Use it a second time only if you want a 60-second rest between locomotion rounds. Block 1 has no clock at all, on purpose.
